tldr: Charrière builds a coding agent live in Go with Genkit and a small local model on Docker Model Runner, showing that one bash tool can replace a catalogue of dedicated tools.
summary: Charrière, a solution architect at Docker, runs everything on a 32 GB MacBook Air with a JetBrains Mellum model that he said has 12B parameters, about 2.5B active per token, served by Docker Model Runner (a wrapper around llama.cpp or vLLM, with a request inspector in Docker Desktop that helps with debugging). He explains function calling: the model only emits a tool name and arguments, and the agent executes the tool. The first demo uses Genkit for Go with four calculator and price-lookup tools for a computer store. The second wraps curl, grep and similar commands as separate tools to fetch example.com and create a Go module. Every extra tool description eats context, which hurts small models, so the third version keeps a single bash tool with a longer description. The model already knows Unix CLIs, and when it doesn't it can run --help.

The final step puts the loop behind a chat prompt, configured from a YAML file, as an agent called Bob, run inside Docker's sbx sandbox (a micro VM with its own Docker engine and a proxy that hides API keys). Bob writes, builds and runs a small Go program. After being told to run gopls help, it uses gopls workspace symbol, references and rename -w to find and rename a method. Next steps he lists: ripgrep or ast-grep, an edit tool, a skills tool, detection of hallucinations and silent endless loops, RAG, context compression by summarising history, and MCP. His side project grew out of this, with guardrails for local models. In Q&A he recommended small Qwen models and Menlo's Lucy and Jan-nano for tool calling.
keyPoints: The model never executes a tool; it returns a tool name and parameters, the agent runs it and appends the result to the message history.
Each extra tool description fills the context window, which hurts small local models far more than hosted ones.
A single bash tool lets the model use curl, grep, find, go mod and go version from its training knowledge, and --help covers CLIs it doesn't know.
With gopls available through bash, the agent finds symbols, references and renames code more precisely than with grep.
Small agents need guards against hallucinated tool calls and silent endless loops, or the program never terminates.
takeaways: Try replacing a pile of narrow tools or MCP servers with one well-described bash tool when context is tight.
Run any agent that has shell access inside a sandbox such as a micro VM, not directly on your laptop.
Add loop detection and context compression before relying on a small local model for agent work.
Point the agent at language-server CLIs like gopls for code navigation and refactoring.

quotes.text: Very important, the model cannot execute any tool. The model can only generate text or data.

watchIf: You use coding agents and want to see how small the core loop is, or want to run one on a local model.
